conclusion.justification: The report concludes with 'no—not reliably, based on current evidence,' highlighting strong trial data showing no benefit over placebo while acknowledging mixed meta-analysis results. Because it takes a cautiously unfavorable stance on the claim, it is classified as leans_reject.
conclusion.label: leans_reject

report:
**Conclusion: no—not reliably, based on current evidence.** Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) is biologically plausible because statins can lower CoQ10 levels, but this has not translated into consistent, clinically convincing relief of statin-associated muscle discomfort.

The strongest caution comes from a randomized crossover trial in people with *confirmed* statin myalgia: 600 mg/day CoQ10 did **not** improve muscle pain, strength, or aerobic performance versus placebo. This matters because muscle symptoms reported while taking a statin are not always caused by the statin.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4298455/

Reviews of trials conflict. A 2018 meta-analysis of randomized trials reported improvement in several self-reported muscle symptoms, but later evidence synthesis found the trial evidence “equivocal”: some studies suggest benefit and others do not. Differences in who was enrolled, symptom definitions, doses, and subjective pain measurement likely contribute to the inconsistency.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30371340/  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9171566/

Thus, CoQ10 may help an individual patient, is generally considered a plausible low-risk trial, but it should not be presented as an established treatment or a reason to stop a statin. If symptoms occur, discuss them with the prescriber: assessment for other causes and adjusting, switching, or rechallenging the statin has a stronger evidence base than relying on CoQ10. Mayo Clinic likewise says more studies are needed.  
https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/high-blood-cholesterol/in-depth/statin-side-effects/art-20046013
